A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LEC framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D support a reliable comparison despite the changed title and expanded evaluation.

before.justification: V1 reports original FDR, power, and routing experiments on CommonsenseQA and TriviaQA, including supplementary uncertainty and sampling analyses.

after.justification: V2 reports original QA experiments and additional ScienceQA and MM-Vet v2 evaluations, routing comparisons, and sensitivity analyses.

M1.justification: The linear calibration constraint, coverage-maximizing threshold selection, and accept/route/abstain procedure remain unchanged. Algorithms 2–3 document these existing procedures; the additional models and uncertainty estimators are evaluation configurations rather than new LEC components.

E1.justification: V2 retains CommonsenseQA and TriviaQA and adds closed-ended ScienceQA and open-ended MM-Vet v2 evaluations. These introduce image-conditioned question answering, substantially extending coverage beyond language-only QA.

E2.justification: The single-model COIN-CP and COIN-HFD comparators are retained under the names UCB-CLP and UCB-HFD. V2 adds evaluated UCB-CLP-Routing, UCB-HFD-Routing, and independently calibrated LEC routing comparators in Figures 6, 20, and 21. V1's comparison against routing without coverage maximization is removed.

E3.justification: TriviaQA increases from 4,000 to 8,000 samples. Semantic-entropy clustering changes from matching the answer-alignment criterion to bi-entailment by default, and the NLI model changes from DeBERTa-large to DeBERTa-v3. The evaluated model configurations also change, and new protocols introduce LLM judging, AUROC, and calibration-split sweeps.

E4.justification: V2 adds joint-versus-independent routing calibration ablations and calibration/test-ratio sensitivity studies. Existing uncertainty, alignment, and sampling analyses are reworked, including SELF, LLM-as-a-Judge, and SE/EigV sampling studies with LLaMA-3.1-70B. The earlier grid-search-versus-best-cover analysis is removed, and uncertainty histograms change from seven models to two.

E5.justification: The reported number of random calibration/test splits increases from 100 to 500. Mean and standard-deviation reporting remains, while new split-ratio boxplots additionally display FDR variability. These are repeated data splits, not reported independent model-training runs.

E6.justification: QA and routing results are extensively revised, alongside new VQA and ablation outcomes. For example, Qwen2.5-14B's TriviaQA LEC power at alpha 0.05 changes from 0.9994 in v1 Table 3 to 0.7193 in v2 Table 1. Changed sample counts and clustering settings preclude interpreting this as a same-setting performance decline.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 explicitly states joint-output exchangeability and adds an argument transferring it to routing indicators. Appendix B replaces an abstract routing index with a formal first-threshold-passing-model definition. The main theorems, calibration bounds, and central proof equations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The linear-constraint formulation, finite-sample FDR claim, and joint-routing contribution remain central. V2 broadens its stated empirical applicability from LLM QA to foundation-model QA/VQA and qualifies routing gains as occurring in favorable regimes, with greater emphasis on allocation and cost tradeoffs.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of UCB conservatism, failures of independently calibrated routing, and relationships between calibration size, variability, and power. It interprets judge-based evaluation as robustness to noisy correctness labels and develops coverage/cost interpretations of routing allocation. The conclusion more explicitly qualifies when routing benefits arise.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds calibration pseudocode, multimodal prompts and processing details, the precise NLI checkpoint, and the Qwen2.5-7B judging prompt and partial-correctness criterion. It newly documents invalid-output filtering and shared-sample evaluation for routing. However, v1's explicit baseline significance level of delta 0.05 is omitted, although v2 Algorithm 1 still requires delta.

R1.justification: V2 adds references supporting multimodal benchmarks and models, OpenChat, uncertainty estimation, and the statistical bounds, while removing the Learn Then Test citation. It gives Jung et al.'s cascaded judges a more direct role in routing comparisons. The overarching positioning against conformal sets and UCB calibration is retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, experimental narrative, conclusion, and substantial portions of Appendix D are rewritten and reorganized. Routing discussion is separated into risk control and allocation, experimental-setting descriptions are reordered, and an Impact Statement is added. The title and terminology also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn and moved to the first page. Aggregated FDR curves and bar charts become per-model comparison panels; power tables and routing-allocation displays move between the main text and appendix. Numerous new displays are added. V2 Figure 9 mismatches reordered plots with model/UQ attributions, and Figure 12 duplicates baseline legend labels.

improvement.justification: The routing baselines, independent-calibration ablation, sensitivity tests, and implementation details strengthen evidence and reproducibility beyond v1. The overall gain is limited: Appendix A retains an unjustified exchangeability step for calibration-dependent thresholds, while v2 introduces Figure 9 attribution errors and ambiguous Figure 12 legends and omits the previously specified baseline significance level. The empirical expansion improves scrutiny without resolving the central proof problem.
